headline: Huang's Nvidia return sparks best stock rally in over a year
summary: U.S. stocks surged on Monday after Nvidia brought Jensen Huang back as CEO, with the [[S&P 500]] up 4.73% for its best day in more than a year and the [[Nasdaq]] up 6.51%. It mattered this much because the market leans on a handful of giant AI-linked companies, so when doubts about Nvidia hit, the whole index suffered, and when the doubts eased, the whole index bounced. The [[VIX]], which measures how nervous traders are, fell 25.83% to 26.62, so a lot of fear drained out in one session even though the level is still elevated. Outside stocks the picture was patchier: oil fell 4.23% to 80.43 as crude kept flowing out of the Persian Gulf, the dollar rose 0.49%, and gold jumped 3.65% for reasons that aren't obvious. The [[10-year yield]] barely moved at 4.92%, because Fed officials are still talking about higher interest rates over time to deal with energy-driven inflation.
one_thing: One personnel decision at one company moved the whole U.S. stock market, which shows how concentrated the market has become in AI. The relief came with real pushback from Congress and open questions about Nvidia, so the rebound is fragile.

cross_asset.stocks: The [[S&P 500]] rose 4.73% to 7237.17, the [[Dow]] rose 3.01% to 49595.31 and the [[Nasdaq]] rose 6.51% to 24089.56, so the more AI-heavy the index, the bigger the jump. That gap exists because Nvidia and the companies that depend on its spending, like Oracle and CoreWeave, carry huge weight in the Nasdaq and the S&P 500. Money also left the usual hiding places, since consumer names like Kroger and Tyson Foods were among the S&P 500's biggest losers as investors sold [[defensive stocks]] to buy tech.
cross_asset.rates: The [[10-year yield]] rose 1 [[basis point]] to 4.92%, which is a tiny move, so bonds mostly shrugged at the stock rally, and that matters because mortgage rates tend to follow the 10-year. The 2-year yield sits at 4.63%, well above the Fed's 3.875% policy rate, which means traders expect the Fed's next move to be up, not down. That leaves the [[yield curve]] (10-year minus 2-year) at +29 basis points, so long-term borrowing still costs more than short-term borrowing.
cross_asset.fx: The [[dollar index]] rose 0.49% to 104.32 on bets that the Fed will stay [[hawkish]], even though sterling and the euro ticked higher early in the day when stock futures rebounded. USD/JPY fell 0.49% to 158.93, so the yen gained a little, and it's not obvious why, since the dollar was stronger against most other currencies. Goldman expects the dollar rally to keep going in the coming months and fade in 2027, but its technical read says the dollar is [[overbought]] and could slow.
cross_asset.commodities: [[WTI crude]] fell 4.23% to 80.43, its lowest close since August, because oil kept flowing out of the Persian Gulf despite continued attacks on shipping. Cheaper oil is good news for gas prices and for [[inflation]], which is exactly what the Fed is worried about right now. Gold jumped 3.65% to 3643.8, which is odd on a day when stocks soared and the dollar rose, and the headlines don't explain it.

storylines.name: AI trade jitters
storylines.backstory: Markets have leaned on the biggest AI-linked tech firms, so doubts about AI hit the whole [[S&P 500]]. Nvidia's CEO left on Nov 12, a selloff followed, official papers warned that AI [[valuation]]s look stretched, and the index fell four straight weeks.
storylines.today: Nvidia's board approved Huang's return, and Reuters reports that Trump pressured the company to do it. The Nasdaq rose 6.51% and the S&P 500 had its best day in more than a year, while Oracle and CoreWeave also jumped because cloud companies like them, along with Nebius and Iren, depend on Nvidia's financing of the AI ecosystem. The cheering came with pushback, because lawmakers of both parties questioned Trump's conclusion that Huang is not a national security risk, Treasury Secretary Bessent reversed his harder line on Nvidia, staff abuse allegations surfaced and a reported SEC probe is in the news. A strategist also warned that Wall Street is not pricing in a [[data center]] slowdown, and HPE posted its strongest growth ever and raised its forecast, yet its stock wavered, which hints that good news is already expected.
storylines.market_link: Huang returns, so investors worry less that the AI spending plan will break, which lifts Nvidia and the companies tied to its money, like Oracle and CoreWeave. Because those stocks are so large, the whole S&P 500 and Nasdaq jump, the [[VIX]] falls, and money leaves defensive stocks like Kroger and Tyson. The catch is that the chain also runs in reverse, so a Washington backlash, a legal problem or a data center slowdown could pull the index down just as fast.
storylines.next_chapter: Watch whether Congress or regulators actually act on Huang and Nvidia, what comes of the reported SEC probe, and whether any sign of a data center slowdown shows up. Also watch whether the rally holds after a one-day jump of this size.
note: The big idea is that Nvidia bringing back Jensen Huang flipped the AI trade from fear to relief in one day, and because AI stocks are so large, the whole [[S&P 500]] had its best day in more than a year.

The why is that the index leans on a few AI giants, so doubt about one company, like the Nov 12 CEO exit, dragged everything down for four weeks, and the return reversed part of that. Oracle and CoreWeave jumped because they rely on Nvidia's money flowing through the AI ecosystem.

The so-what is that the rally is fragile, since both parties in Congress are pushing back, an SEC probe is reported, and HPE's record growth didn't lift its stock, so good news may already be in the price.
Interview line: 'Today showed how concentrated the market is, because one CEO headline moved the S&P 500 almost 5%.'

storylines.name: Central banks vs energy inflation
storylines.backstory: The Iran war cut oil supply and pushed up [[headline inflation]], so central banks must decide whether the price jump fades or leaks into wages and services. Euro area inflation hit 4%, the Bank of England hiked to 4% and the Fed sits at 3.875%.
storylines.today: Fed's John Williams said higher interest rates are likely 'over time' to address inflation, but he is confident inflation gets closer to 2% in 2027. Waller said the Fed meets Dec 8 and 9, with the economic outlook discussed on the first day and the policy decision on the second. Cook said damaged infrastructure and low inventories could keep oil prices high for a long time, and Japan's core inflation hit its highest this year as an energy subsidy ended. Meanwhile Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is described as seeing an AI revolution coming that raises hard questions on jobs and interest rates.
storylines.market_link: Oil stays high, so inflation stays high, so Fed officials talk about higher rates, which keeps the 2-year yield at 4.63%, well above the Fed's 3.875% policy rate. Higher rates make holding dollars more rewarding, so the dollar gets support. A San Francisco Fed study adds that when inflation comes from supply problems like oil, Fed surprises tend to move longer-term yields less, which helps explain why the 10-year barely moved today.
storylines.next_chapter: The Dec 8 and 9 Fed meeting is the next big test, and in the meantime, cheaper oil would make the case for hikes weaker while strong growth and income data would make it stronger.
note: The big idea is that energy prices are keeping central banks cautious, so the Fed is leaning toward higher rates over time even though Williams expects inflation to get closer to 2% in 2027.
The why is that oil-driven inflation can spread into wages and services, and central banks hike to stop that, so a 2-year yield well above the Fed's rate means traders are betting on hikes.
The so-what is that the Dec 8 and 9 meeting will decide whether talk turns into action, and today's oil drop gives officials a little more room to wait.
Interview line: 'Supply-driven inflation is hard for the Fed because hiking doesn't fix an oil shortage, so it mostly moves short-term yields and the dollar.'

storylines.name: Iran war and oil
storylines.backstory: The conflict began in early 2026 and cut global oil output by 12 mb/d in March, but prices stayed below records because stored oil filled the gap. The IEA says the Hormuz shock lifted the world's oil and gas import bill 25% to $1.6 trillion.
storylines.today: [[WTI crude]] fell 4.23% to 80.43, its lowest close since August, because oil kept flowing out of the Persian Gulf even though tanker attacks continue. A headline says China has become the top oil buyer. Trump suggested the recent drop in gas prices is driven by political forces now that the midterms are over, and a headline puts the phrase 'a giant hoax' on it.
storylines.market_link: Oil keeps flowing, so the supply fear fades, so crude gets cheaper. Cheaper crude means lower gas prices for drivers and lower costs for businesses, which should cool inflation and give the Fed less reason to hike. The catch is that Cook warned damaged infrastructure and low inventories could keep prices high for a long time, so the relief may not last.
storylines.next_chapter: Watch whether Gulf exports keep flowing despite tanker attacks, whether China's buying keeps demand strong, and whether crude stays below the August level it just reached.
note: The big idea is that oil dropped to its lowest close since August because Persian Gulf crude is still reaching buyers despite attacks on ships.
The why is that markets price what actually arrives, not what might be threatened, so steady flows pull prices down even in a war. Stored oil also helped fill the gap earlier this year.
The so-what is that lower oil helps inflation and gas prices, but Cook's warning about damaged infrastructure and low inventories means the drop could reverse.
Interview line: 'Oil is trading on flows, not headlines, and today the flows won.'

storylines.name: US midterms and the dollar
storylines.backstory: The midterms produced what headlines call a Democratic rout, and markets asked how divided government might change tariffs, spending and the [[dollar index]]. The dollar then had its biggest rally since 2024.
storylines.today: The dollar index rose 0.49% to 104.32, and headlines credit hawkish Fed bets, not the election. Goldman Sachs expects the rally to continue in the coming months and fade in 2027, though its technical read says the dollar is [[overbought]] and could slow. Sterling and the euro edged up in the morning as the stock rebound took some of the shine off the dollar, but the dollar was higher again by the close.
storylines.market_link: Fed officials signal higher rates, so traders expect U.S. rates to stay above those elsewhere, which makes dollars more attractive to hold and pushes the dollar up. A stronger dollar makes imports cheaper for Americans but makes dollar debts and commodities pricier for the rest of the world. The catch is that when the dollar has run this far, even a small change in Fed talk can slow it.
storylines.next_chapter: Watch whether the Dec 8 and 9 Fed meeting backs up the hawkish bets, and whether the overbought signal Goldman flagged turns into a pause or a pullback.
note: The big idea is that the dollar is rising because of Fed expectations, not the midterm election, even though the election started the conversation.
The why is that higher expected U.S. interest rates pay holders of dollars more, so money flows toward the dollar, and today the index rose 0.49% to 104.32.
The so-what is that Goldman sees the rally continuing for months and fading in 2027, but its own technical read says the dollar is stretched, so the next leg may be slower.
Interview line: 'This dollar rally is a rates story, so I'd watch the Fed meeting, not the election.'

stories.title: One CEO's return lifts the whole market
stories.what: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, and the S&P 500 jumped 4.73% while the Nasdaq rose 6.51%. Oracle and CoreWeave also surged on the bet that Nvidia's financing of the AI ecosystem keeps going.
stories.why: A handful of AI firms now carry so much of the index that confidence in Nvidia works like confidence in the whole market. That is why the VIX fell 25.83% in a day.
stories.watch: Watch for any slowdown in data center spending, because a strategist warned the market isn't pricing one in.

stories.title: Congress pushes back on Huang's return
stories.what: Lawmakers of both parties questioned Trump's conclusion that Huang is not a national security risk, and Reuters says Trump pressured Nvidia to bring him back. Bessent also reversed a harder line on Nvidia, and a reported SEC probe and staff abuse allegations are in the news.
stories.why: The rally rests on the idea that the AI trade is safe again, so political or legal trouble around the most important AI company could undo it quickly.
stories.watch: Watch for hearings, letters or regulatory steps aimed at Nvidia.

stories.title: Safe stocks lose out as tech roars back
stories.what: Consumer stocks like Kroger and Tyson Foods were among the S&P 500's biggest losers while Nvidia stormed higher. Canada's TSX also ended a seven-session losing streak as base metals and technology stocks surged.
stories.why: Investors had been hiding in safe, steady stocks during the AI scare, so when the fear faded they sold those shelters to buy growth, which is a classic sign of a risk-on day.
stories.watch: Watch whether defensive stocks keep lagging, because a reversal would hint that the fear is coming back.

stories.title: Crude falls to its lowest close since August
stories.what: WTI crude fell 4.23% to 80.43 because oil kept flowing out of the Persian Gulf despite continued attacks on shipping. A headline also says China has become the top oil buyer.
stories.why: Cheaper oil lowers gas prices and eases pressure on inflation, which gives central banks less reason to hike. It also shows markets care more about barrels that arrive than about scary headlines.
stories.watch: Watch for Cook's warning to come true, since damaged infrastructure and low inventories could keep prices high for a long time.

stories.title: Fed officials keep rate hikes on the table
stories.what: Williams said higher rates are likely over time to address inflation, though he expects inflation to get closer to 2% in 2027. Waller noted the Fed meets Dec 8 and 9.
stories.why: The 2-year yield at 4.63% sits well above the Fed's 3.875% rate, so traders already expect hikes, and that supports the dollar and keeps borrowing costs high for households and businesses.
stories.watch: Watch the Dec 8 and 9 meeting and the GDP and personal income data due this week.

under_the_radar.title: ECB opens the door to tokenised collateral
under_the_radar.what: The ECB's Governing Council approved accepting assets issued on licensed digital ledger platforms as eligible collateral for Eurosystem credit operations. Details are due in spring 2027, with implementation planned for June 2027.
under_the_radar.chain: [[Collateral]] is what banks hand to the central bank to borrow cash, so a longer list of accepted assets makes tokenised bonds more useful. That could make them cheaper to issue, which could slowly move more of the plumbing of euro markets onto these new systems. The effect on rates or the euro is small and slow for now.
under_the_radar.watch: Watch for the technical requirements in spring 2027 and whether banks actually start pledging these assets after June 2027.
note: The big idea is that the ECB is making room for tokenised assets in its collateral rules, but only with strict safety standards.
The why is that collateral is the backbone of central bank lending, so if an asset can be pledged, it becomes more useful and easier to sell.
The so-what is that this is slow plumbing news, not a market mover today, but it shows central banks adapting to new technology.
Interview line: 'The ECB is widening what counts as collateral while keeping the same risk standards.'

under_the_radar.title: US labor supply may soon start shrinking
under_the_radar.what: A New York Fed note says growth in the U.S. working-age population has fallen to near zero because net immigration dropped sharply, and the native-born working-age population keeps declining. Other advanced economies went through similar trends, and many offset them with higher participation, for example Japan's labor force grew about 6% while its working-age population fell about 7%.
under_the_radar.chain: Fewer available workers means employers compete harder for the people who are there, so wages can rise, which can keep service prices rising. That matters because the Fed's big question right now is whether energy-driven inflation leaks into wages, so a shrinking labor pool would make that leak more likely and strengthen the case for higher rates.
under_the_radar.watch: Watch wage growth, labor force participation and any Fed comments linking labor supply to inflation.
note: The big idea is that the pool of U.S. workers may stop growing and could soon shrink because immigration has dropped and the native-born working-age population is declining.
The why is that other countries faced this earlier and mostly kept their labor forces growing by getting more women and older workers to participate.
The so-what is that a tight labor supply can push wages up, which would keep inflation sticky and the Fed more hawkish.
Interview line: 'Labor supply is a quiet inflation driver, because fewer workers means more wage pressure.'

under_the_radar.title: Lagarde says act before the problem is obvious
under_the_radar.what: In Frankfurt on Nov 20, Lagarde said it was her last time speaking at this banking congress as ECB president, which hints at a leadership change, although the timing isn't clear. She argued that policymakers should act early and used Machiavelli's image of a fever that is easy to cure but hard to detect at first, and easy to detect but hard to cure later.
under_the_radar.chain: The speech is mostly about making Europe stronger and less dependent on others, not about the next rate move, so it shouldn't be over-read. Still, if that act-early mindset carried into rate decisions with euro area inflation at 4% and the ECB at 2.5%, it would favor tightening sooner, which would lift euro yields and support the euro.
under_the_radar.watch: Watch for ECB signals on whether 4% inflation is seen as temporary, and for news on who leads the ECB next.
note: The big idea is that Lagarde's farewell-style speech stressed acting early, because problems are cheapest to fix before they are obvious.
The why is that acting early means paying a cost now for a benefit later, and if nothing goes wrong it can look like a waste.
The so-what is that the speech doesn't announce a policy move, but it gives a clue about how the ECB thinks about risks like energy inflation.
Interview line: 'Central banks face a timing problem, because waiting for proof often means acting too late.'

deep_dive.why_now: Oracle and CoreWeave jumped on the bet that AI money keeps flowing, and this St. Louis Fed piece shows who is actually paying for the AI buildout.
key_points: The study looks at ten large tech firms it calls [[hyperscalers]], including Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Nvidia and Oracle, and tracks how they pay for their AI investment.

Their debt compared with assets fell from nearly 30% in 2023 to roughly 25% in early 2026, while other public U.S. firms stayed near 34%, so the spending has been funded mostly from profits rather than borrowing.
Their payouts to shareholders fell from about 4% of assets in 2022 to about 2% by early 2026, which means they are keeping more cash at home.
Data center builders lean more heavily on debt and have cut payouts, while chip suppliers cover more modest investment with operating cash flow.
The analysis misses off-balance-sheet commitments like leases and purchase obligations, which may be a large part of data center builders' future plans.
deep_dive.market_angle: Strong balance sheets at the biggest firms mean the AI boom is less likely to crack because of a funding problem, which supports Nvidia and big tech. Cloud and data center builders like Oracle and CoreWeave are more exposed to borrowing costs, so rising yields or tighter credit would hit them first.
deep_dive.trade_idea: A desk might go long a basket of cash-rich chip suppliers and big tech against a basket of debt-funded data center builders, a [[pair trade]] that gains if funding conditions tighten. The main risk is another day like today, when risk appetite surges and the weaker builders rally harder, squeezing the short side.
note: The big idea is that the biggest AI spenders are mostly paying with their own profits, not heavy borrowing.
The why is that their debt compared with assets fell to about 25% from nearly 30%, while the average U.S. firm stayed near 34%, so they look financially strong.
The so-what is that the weak link is the data center builders, who borrow more and have commitments that don't show on the balance sheet.
Interview line: 'The AI boom is financed mostly by cash flow at the top, but the builders further down the chain lean on debt.'

deep_dive.why_now: Fed officials are talking about higher rates while oil-driven inflation is mostly a supply story, and this San Francisco Fed letter explains why that changes how bond markets react.
key_points: The Fed responds more aggressively to demand-driven inflation than to supply-driven inflation, in line with its balanced approach when its jobs and price goals conflict.
Researchers tracked the surprise part of Fed announcements and found it passes through to longer-term forward rates mainly when inflation is demand-driven.
They split inflation into supply and demand by checking whether prices and quantities move in the same direction, which points to demand, or in opposite directions, which points to supply.
The supply component tends to follow food and energy prices, so an oil shock is mostly a supply story.
Because supply pressures have come back, Fed surprises are likely to have a smaller effect on longer-horizon yields.
deep_dive.market_angle: Hawkish Fed talk should move short-term yields like the 2-year and the dollar more than the 10-year, which fits why the 10-year barely budged today. That tends to flatten the yield curve, meaning the gap between long and short yields shrinks.
deep_dive.trade_idea: A desk might consider a curve flattener, selling 2-year Treasuries against buying 10-year Treasuries, which gains if hawkish Fed talk lifts short yields more than long ones. The main risk is that oil keeps falling and the Fed backs off, which would pull the 2-year down faster and steepen the curve, and the research describes an average pattern, not a guarantee.
note: The big idea is that the source of inflation changes how much a Fed move affects long-term yields.
The why is that markets know the Fed can't fix an oil shortage with rates, so Fed surprises during supply shocks matter less for longer-term yields.
The so-what is that the 2-year and the dollar are the places to look for Fed news right now, while the 10-year may stay calmer.
Interview line: 'When inflation is supply-driven, the Fed's reach into long-term yields is weaker.'

The index's 4.73% jump was its best day in more than a year, and the Nasdaq's 6.51% gain shows where the money went.

Fear drained out fast, since the [[VIX]] fell 25.83% to 26.62 and money moved out of defensive stocks like Kroger and Tyson into tech. Canada's TSX also ended a seven-session losing streak, so the relief was not just an American story.

Bonds barely reacted, with the [[10-year yield]] up just 1 basis point to 4.92%, because the Fed's message is still about higher rates over time. The 2-year yield at 4.63% sits about 75 basis points above the Fed's 3.875% rate, which means traders expect hikes.

Oil fell 4.23% to its lowest close since August because Gulf crude kept flowing, which helps inflation, while the dollar rose 0.49% on Fed bets. Gold's 3.65% jump and the yen's small gain are not clearly explained by the headlines.
Interview line: 'Today was an AI concentration day, with one CEO headline moving the S&P 500 almost 5%, while rates and the dollar kept saying the Fed is more likely to hike than cut.'
take: Nvidia's Huang return sent the Nasdaq up 6.51% in one day, so would you chase that rally, fade it, or stay out in the Nasdaq, how big would you make the position, and what specific event (for example Congress forcing a change, the reported SEC probe or a sign of a data center slowdown) would prove you wrong?

10-year yield.def: The interest rate the U.S. government pays to borrow money for ten years. Mortgage rates and many business loans tend to follow it.
10-year yield.analogy: It's like the interest rate on a ten-year loan to the government.
10-year yield.today: The 10-year yield rose just 1 basis point to 4.92%, so bonds mostly ignored the huge stock rally.

Collateral.def: Something of value that a borrower hands over to protect the lender in case the loan isn't repaid. Banks pledge collateral to central banks when they borrow cash.
Collateral.analogy: It's like leaving your car title with a lender until you pay them back.
Collateral.today: The ECB said it will accept assets issued on licensed digital ledger platforms as collateral, with details due in spring 2027 and implementation planned for June 2027.

Dow.def: The Dow Jones Industrial Average is an index of 30 large U.S. companies. It's one of the oldest ways to take the temperature of the stock market.
Dow.analogy: It's like a school report card that only grades 30 of the biggest students.
Dow.today: The Dow rose 3.01% to 49595.31, a strong day but smaller than the Nasdaq's gain because it holds fewer AI-heavy companies.

Nasdaq.def: The Nasdaq Composite is an index packed with technology and growth companies. It tends to swing more than the broader market when tech is in the news.
Nasdaq.analogy: It's like the team's star forwards, who score the most but also take the most risk.
Nasdaq.today: The Nasdaq jumped 6.51% to 24089.56, the biggest gain of the major indexes, because Nvidia and other AI names led the rally.

S&P 500.def: An index that tracks 500 of the largest U.S. companies, weighted by size. Investors treat it as the main scoreboard for the U.S. stock market.
S&P 500.analogy: It's like a class average where the biggest companies count the most.
S&P 500.today: The S&P 500 rose 4.73% to 7237.17, its best day in more than a year, because a few giant AI-linked companies carry so much weight.

VIX.def: A gauge of how much traders expect the S&P 500 to swing over the next month. It rises when people are nervous and falls when they relax.
VIX.analogy: It's like a nervousness meter for the stock market.
VIX.today: The VIX fell 25.83% to 26.62, so a lot of fear drained out in one day, although the level is still elevated.

WTI crude.def: West Texas Intermediate is the main U.S. benchmark price for a barrel of oil. It influences what gasoline and many other fuels cost.
WTI crude.analogy: It's like the sticker price that sets the tone for everything made from oil.
WTI crude.today: WTI fell 4.23% to 80.43, its lowest close since August, because Persian Gulf oil kept flowing despite attacks on ships.

basis point.def: One hundredth of a percentage point. Traders use it to describe small changes in interest rates.
basis point.analogy: It's like measuring a short walk in inches instead of miles.
basis point.today: The 10-year yield rose 1 basis point, which is a tiny move, while the yield curve sits at +29 basis points.

data center.def: A huge building full of computers that stores data and runs AI programs. Companies spend enormous sums building and powering them.
data center.analogy: It's like a giant factory where the product is computing power.
data center.today: A strategist warned that Wall Street isn't pricing in a data center slowdown, so a drop in building plans would be a surprise for stocks like Nvidia, Oracle and CoreWeave.

defensive stocks.def: Shares of companies like grocers and food makers whose sales hold up even when the economy or markets get shaky. Investors tend to hide in them when they're scared.
defensive stocks.analogy: It's like a storm shelter that people leave once the weather clears.
defensive stocks.today: Kroger and Tyson Foods were among the S&P 500's biggest losers because investors sold these shelters to buy tech.

dollar index.def: A measure of the U.S. dollar against a basket of major currencies. When it rises, the dollar is getting stronger.
dollar index.analogy: It's like a scoreboard that shows how the dollar is doing against its rivals.
dollar index.today: The dollar index rose 0.49% to 104.32 as traders bet that the Fed will stay hawkish.

hawkish.def: Favoring higher interest rates or a tougher stance to fight inflation. The opposite is dovish, which favors lower rates.
hawkish.analogy: It's like a coach who keeps the pressure on even when the team wants a break.
hawkish.today: Williams said higher rates are likely over time, which is a hawkish message and helps explain why the 2-year yield is 4.63%.

headline inflation.def: The overall rise in prices, including food and energy, which are the items that jump around the most. It differs from core inflation, which leaves those out.
headline inflation.analogy: It's like the full grocery bill including the items whose prices change every week.
headline inflation.today: Euro area headline inflation is at 4%, which is why central banks worry that the oil shock will spread.

hyperscalers.def: The giant tech companies that run huge data centers or supply the chips inside them. The St. Louis Fed uses the word for ten big firms including Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Nvidia and Oracle.
hyperscalers.analogy: They're like the biggest landlords in the world of cloud computing.
hyperscalers.today: A St. Louis Fed study found these firms mostly pay for AI with their own profits, since their debt compared with assets fell from nearly 30% in 2023 to roughly 25% in early 2026.

inflation.def: The rate at which prices across the economy rise over time. When it's high, your money buys less than it used to.
inflation.analogy: It's like your paycheck slowly shrinking at the checkout line.
inflation.today: Cheaper oil should ease inflation, which matters because the Fed is deciding whether energy-driven price rises will spread.

overbought.def: A signal that something has risen so fast that it may be due for a pause or a small pullback.
overbought.analogy: It's like a runner who sprinted the first mile and needs to catch their breath.
overbought.today: Goldman's technical read says the dollar is overbought even though it expects the rally to continue in the coming months.

pair trade.def: A trade that bets on one asset rising and a related one falling at the same time. The goal is to profit from the difference between them.
pair trade.analogy: It's like betting that one runner beats another, no matter how fast the race goes.
pair trade.today: A desk could buy cash-rich chip suppliers and big tech while selling debt-funded data center builders, which pays off if funding gets tighter.

valuation.def: How expensive a stock is compared with what the company earns or is expected to earn. High valuations mean investors are paying a lot for future growth.
valuation.analogy: It's like the price tag on a house compared with the rent it earns.
valuation.today: Official papers have warned that AI valuations look stretched, which is part of why doubts about Nvidia hit the whole market so hard.

yield curve.def: A line showing how interest rates change from short-term to long-term government loans. Its shape tells you what traders expect for the economy and the Fed.
yield curve.analogy: It's like a price list that charges different rates depending on how long you borrow.
yield curve.today: The 10-year minus 2-year gap is +29 basis points, so long-term borrowing still costs more than short-term borrowing.

steps.label: Huang returns
steps.explain: Nvidia's board approved Jensen Huang's return as CEO, reportedly after pressure from Trump.
steps.detail: Huang left on Nov 12, and that exit set off a selloff and four straight weekly losses for the S&P 500. His return told investors that the leader of the most important AI company is back.

steps.label: AI stocks jump
steps.explain: Nvidia and companies that rely on its money, like Oracle and CoreWeave, surged.
steps.detail: Cloud companies such as Oracle, CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren depend on Nvidia's financing of the AI ecosystem. If Nvidia is stable, that cash is more likely to keep flowing.

steps.label: Nasdaq surges
steps.explain: The Nasdaq rose 6.51% because it holds so many AI-linked giants.
steps.detail: The more tech-heavy an index is, the bigger its jump, which is why the Nasdaq beat the Dow. A move this large in one session shows how much the market leans on a few names.

steps.label: S&P 500 best day
steps.explain: The S&P 500 rose 4.73%, its best day in more than a year.
steps.detail: Big AI-linked companies make up a huge slice of the S&P 500, so their jump lifts the whole index. Consumer names like Kroger and Tyson fell as money left defensive stocks for tech.

steps.label: Fear drains
steps.explain: The VIX fell 25.83% to 26.62 as traders relaxed.
steps.detail: When stocks stop falling, traders pay less for protection against big swings, so the VIX drops. It's still at an elevated level, which means nerves haven't fully settled.

steps.label: Gulf crude keeps flowing
steps.explain: Oil kept leaving the Persian Gulf even though attacks on tankers continue.
steps.detail: Markets price the barrels that actually reach buyers, not just the threat to them. Stored oil also helped fill the gap earlier this year.

steps.label: WTI falls
steps.explain: WTI crude dropped 4.23% to 80.43, its lowest close since August.
steps.detail: When traders see supply arriving, they stop paying extra to protect against a shortage. That pulls the price of a barrel down.

steps.label: Inflation pressure eases
steps.explain: Cheaper oil lowers gas prices and business costs, which cools inflation.
steps.detail: Energy feeds into almost everything, from a drive to the store to the cost of shipping goods. When it gets cheaper, the price jump that started with the Iran war is less likely to spread.

steps.label: Fed hike case weakens
steps.explain: With less inflation pressure, the Fed has a little less reason to raise rates.
steps.detail: Fed officials are worried the energy price jump could leak into wages and services. Cheaper oil gives them more room to wait, although Cook warned that damaged infrastructure and low inventories could keep prices high for a long time.

steps.label: Fed talks hikes
steps.explain: Williams said higher interest rates are likely over time to address inflation.
steps.detail: Williams also said he is confident inflation gets closer to 2% in 2027, so he's not predicting a crisis. Still, the message is that rates are more likely to go up than down.

steps.label: Short yields stay high
steps.explain: The 2-year yield sits at 4.63%, well above the Fed's 3.875% policy rate.
steps.detail: The 2-year yield reflects where traders think the Fed's rate will be over the next two years. Being 75 basis points above today's rate means traders expect hikes.

steps.label: Dollar gains
steps.explain: Higher expected U.S. rates make holding dollars more rewarding, so the dollar index rose 0.49% to 104.32.
steps.detail: Investors move money toward the currency that pays more. Goldman expects the rally to continue for months, although its technical read says the dollar is overbought.

steps.label: 10-year barely moves
steps.explain: The 10-year yield rose only 1 basis point to 4.92%.
steps.detail: A San Francisco Fed study found that Fed surprises reach long-term yields less when inflation comes from supply problems like oil. That fits today, since the Fed can raise rates but it can't pump more oil.

quiz.q: The Dow rose 3.01% while the Nasdaq rose 6.51%. What best explains the gap?
options: The Dow was dragged down by a jump in the 10-year yield
The Nasdaq holds more consumer stocks that investors rushed into
The Nasdaq holds more AI-linked giants that Huang's return lifted most
The Dow holds more energy producers that fell with crude prices
quiz.explain: Nvidia and the companies that depend on its spending carry heavy weight in the Nasdaq, so the AI relief rally showed up there most. The 10-year yield rose only 1 basis point, so it wasn't a drag.

quiz.q: Kroger and Tyson Foods were among the S&P 500's biggest losers while Nvidia soared. What best explains that?
options: A jump in bond yields made grocery stocks less appealing
Investors sold steady defensive names to buy growth as fear faded
Higher oil prices raised their costs and hurt their profit outlook
Lawmakers started targeting food companies after Huang's return
quiz.explain: Investors had been hiding in safe stocks during the AI scare, so when fear faded they sold those shelters to buy tech. Oil actually fell 4.23% and the 10-year yield barely moved.

quiz.q: The BOJ chief has signaled a near-term hike. If the BOJ raises rates and narrows its gap with the Fed's 3.875%, what would USD/JPY, now 158.93, probably do?
options: Up
Down
quiz.explain: A higher Japanese rate makes holding yen more rewarding, so fewer traders sell yen for dollars and the yen strengthens. That pushes USD/JPY down.

quiz.q: Fed officials sound more hawkish about oil-driven inflation than traders expected. What would the 2-year yield, now 4.63%, probably do?
options: Up
Down
quiz.explain: The 2-year yield tracks expected Fed rates over the next two years, so tougher talk pushes it up. The San Francisco Fed research says the 10-year would react less because the inflation is supply-driven.

quiz.q: Reports of a formal SEC action against Nvidia hit while the VIX sits at 26.62. What would the VIX probably do?
options: Up
Down
quiz.explain: The rebound rests on the AI trade feeling safe again, so legal trouble at Nvidia would bring nerves back. Traders then pay more for protection and the VIX rises.

quiz.q: Put today's AI stock chain in the right cause-and-effect order.
items: S&P 500 posts its best day in over a year
quiz.explain: The personnel news came first, the AI-linked stocks reacted, their weight lifted the index, and the calmer market drained fear from the VIX.

quiz.q: Put today's oil chain in the right cause-and-effect order.
items: Gulf crude keeps flowing despite tanker attacks
WTI closes at its lowest since August
Gas prices and inflation pressure ease
Fed has less reason to hike
quiz.explain: Steady supply came first, so crude got cheaper, which eases inflation worries and gives the Fed a bit more room to wait.

quiz.q: The dollar index rose 0.49% to 104.32 mainly because investors reacted to the Democratic midterm rout.
options: True
False
quiz.explain: The midterms started the dollar conversation, but headlines credit hawkish Fed bets for today's gain.

quiz.q: The 2-year yield at 4.63% sitting well above the Fed's 3.875% rate suggests traders expect the Fed's next move to be a hike.
options: True
False
quiz.explain: Short-term yields follow expected policy rates, so a 2-year yield about 75 basis points above the Fed's rate means traders are betting on higher rates.

quiz.q: The St. Louis Fed found that the big AI spenders' debt compared with assets rose from about 25% in 2023 to nearly 30% in early 2026.
options: True
False
quiz.explain: The direction is backwards. Their ratio fell from nearly 30% to roughly 25%, so the spending has been funded mostly from profits.

quiz.q: Fed officials talked about higher rates over time, yet the 10-year yield rose only 1 basis point to 4.92%. Which explanation fits best?
options: Bond traders ignored the Fed because the stock rally absorbed all the buying
Williams said inflation will near 2% in 2027, which erased every hike bet
The 2-year yield fell enough to cancel out the rise in long-term yields
Oil-driven inflation is a supply problem, so Fed surprises reach long-term yields less
quiz.explain: The San Francisco Fed letter found Fed surprises pass through to longer yields mainly when inflation is demand-driven. Hike bets haven't disappeared, since the 2-year still sits well above the Fed's rate.

quiz.q: Cook warned that damaged infrastructure and low inventories could keep oil prices high for a long time. Why does that matter after WTI's 4.23% drop?
options: It means oil company stocks should fall more than crude itself
It suggests the relief could fade, so inflation worries might return
It shows Gulf tankers have stopped moving, which explains the drop
It means the Fed will cut rates now that oil is cheaper
quiz.explain: Today's drop came from steady flows, but Cook's point is that the underlying supply is still fragile. That means cheaper oil may not last, and neither would the relief for inflation.

quiz.q: The VIX fell 25.83% to 26.62. What does that say about the mood in the market?
options: Traders are buying more protection because the index rose so far
Traders expect smaller swings than before, but nerves are still high
Traders expect the S&P 500 to keep rising after such a big jump
Traders see volatility as gone now that the index has bounced back
quiz.explain: A falling VIX means traders expect calmer markets, so fear drained out. The level is still elevated, so the market hasn't fully relaxed.

quiz.q: Why does the gap between the Fed's 3.875% and the BOJ's 1.25% keep pressure on the yen?
options: Low Japanese rates push foreign investors to buy yen as a haven
Japan prints extra yen to buy dollars whenever rates diverge
Japan sells dollars each day until the rate gap closes by itself
Holding dollars pays more than holding yen, so traders sell yen
quiz.explain: A 2.625 percentage point gap rewards traders for holding dollars instead of yen, so they sell yen. Japan's intervention goes the other way, since it sells dollars to buy yen.

quiz.q: A New York Fed note says U.S. labor supply may soon shrink. Why does that matter for the Fed's energy inflation worry?
options: Fewer workers lets wages rise, so energy inflation could spread to services
Fewer workers means higher company profits, so stocks would rise
Fewer workers lowers growth, so the Fed would cut rates sooner
Fewer workers means less oil demand, so inflation would cool faster
quiz.explain: When employers compete for fewer workers, wages can rise, which can keep service prices climbing. That's exactly the leak into wages and services that central banks fear from the oil shock.

quiz.q: The ECB said it expects to publish the details of its new collateral requirements for tokenised assets in spring 2027, with implementation planned for June 2027.
options: True
False
quiz.explain: That's right, which is why the decision is slow plumbing news rather than something that moves rates or the euro today.
